newsitem.title: USA: Large U.S. crops, 2.4 percent food price rise in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Large U.S. crops, 2.4 percent food price rise in 1997.

text.p: U.S. farmers will open the throttle on output in 1997, the first year of the "Freedom to Farm" law, producing abundant crops and opening an era of modest increases in food prices, the Agriculture Department said Monday.
Food prices were forecast to rise 2.5 percent to 3 percent this year, a relief from 1996's 3.3 percent -- the biggest gain this decade and the first to exceed the overall inflation rate since 1990.

Ample meat and dairy supplies will dampen food inflation this year, chief economist Keith Collins said at the department's annual Outlook Forum. He warned that poor crops -- if they occurred -- could exacerbate cattle culling and "set the stage for a serious increase in retail beef and other meat prices in 1998."

Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman used a keynote speech to warn the European Union against excessive use of export subsidies as well as to crow that "the outlook for American agriculture is very, very good."

U.S.-EU relations have turned prickly in recent months as competition for export sales intensified. The United States has not subsidised a grain sale since July 1995, but Glickman said, "we can't hold out unilaterally forever."
A top-ranking EU administrator, D.F. Roberts, said in remarks that Europe had "neither the budgetary resources nor the intention" of provoking an export war with the United States.

Exports provide nearly 25 cents out of every dollar in U.S. farm receipts. The export market is commonly regarded as the road to prosperity for U.S. agriculture because of rapidly growing food demand around the world.
U.S. agricultural exports would total $56.5 billion this fiscal year, $1 billion more than initially thought, thanks to voracious demand for cotton and soybeans, Glickman said.
Even so, exports would be smaller than the record $59.8 billion of last year. Grain and oilseed prices are lower than last summer when stockpiles were slim worldwide.
The new "Freedom to Farm" law removes most federal controls on farming, letting farmers shift from crop to crop or expand acreage to pursue profits.
For this year, it would mean more corn, wheat and soybeans than last year but less cotton and rice. Export tonnage would be strong and thin U.S. stockpiles would swell modestly.

The size of the wheat recovery was somewhat debatable. Winter wheat seedings, at 48 million acres, were the lowest since 1978. Large spring wheat sowings would be needed to reach the department's forecast of 72 million acres of wheat overall.

Corn output was pegged at 9.63 billion bushels, which would be the second largest crop ever; wheat roughly the same as last year's crop at 2.28 billion bushels; soybeans at 2.5 billion bushels; cotton at 17.3 million bales; and rice at 166.1 million hundredweight. It would be the third decline in a row for rice.

By comparison, output last year was 9.29 billion bushels of corn; 2.28 billion bushels of wheat; 2.38 billion bushels of soybeans; 18.95 million bales of cotton -- the second largest crop on record -- and 171.3 million hundredweight of rice.

Beef production, mimicking a drop in cattle numbers, was forecast to fall by 0.8 percent this year, to 25.4 billion pounds. Pork would rise 2 percent to 17.5 billion pounds and broiler chicken output would be 27.8 billion pounds, up 5.8 percent.
